hazards.channel-wade: You waded past the curtain into open water to reach the far side of the reach. The curtain marks the edge of a controlled work zone for a reason: past it the bottom drops away and the same current the curtain is built to resist is the current that takes a person off their feet. A boat crosses open water; nobody wades it.
hazards.curtain-gap: You left the curtain's overlap seam unclipped. A turbidity curtain is only as good as its weakest joint, and an open seam is a wider hole than the rest of the curtain closed — every log and bag placed after this point stirs sediment straight through the gap into water the 401 certification measures against a limit, not an intention.
hazards.manual-lift-rootwad: You went to muscle the root wad up by hand instead of walking it in on the tag line. A root wad this size is a wet, unbalanced load with no grip anywhere on it; a back is not rated for it and there is no come-along for a strained back once it happens. It moves on a line, at a walking pace, or it does not move today.
hazards.silt-fence-breach: You cut a shortcut through the silt fence to save a walk around with the wheelbarrow. The fence is the only thing between the upland spoil pile and the reach on the next rain, and a foot-wide gap in it is a foot-wide channel for everything upslope to wash straight down into the exact water the curtain in front of you is also trying to protect.

interrupts.alert: The ebb has stalled early and the tide staff at the water's edge shows the flat is already turning — there is far less bare mud out there than the table promised.
interrupts.cue: The water is coming back sooner than planned. Read the staff, not the table.
interrupts.missNote: The crew kept working the table's schedule while the real tide came in around their boots, and coir and shell bags went in half-soaked with nobody able to tell what had been set and what the water had already moved for them. Reading the staff afterward does not undo a tide that already turned.
interrupts.why: A tide table is a prediction built on the moon and an average; wind and barometric pressure push the real water by tens of minutes either way on an ordinary day. The staff gauge is what the water is actually doing right now, and it is the only thing worth trusting once the two disagree — the flat does not care what the table said, it cares what the water is doing.
interrupts.wrongNote: That is not it. The tide staff at the water's edge is the only true reading of where the water actually is right now — nothing else on this bank tells you that.

interrupts.alert: A tug's wake off the channel has set the turbidity curtain surging, and its downstream anchor is walking loose along the mud.
interrupts.cue: Your curtain is coming off its line. Re-tension it before it drags clear.
interrupts.missNote: The anchor kept walking and the curtain lifted off the bottom on the next wake, and the afternoon's turbidity went straight past the one control the permit was relying on — exactly the reading the Water Board's own downstream station would have caught and logged as a violation.
interrupts.why: The curtain only does the job its permit assumes while its anchors hold it against the bottom; an anchor that has walked loose opens a gap the next wake finds first, and everything the crew has stirred up this afternoon goes straight out through it into water the 401 certification exists to protect. It is re-tensioned the moment it is seen dragging, not watched to see whether it settles on its own.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the curtain's own anchor turnbuckle. Nothing else on this bank puts the skirt back down against the bottom.

lateNotes.cordgrass-plugs: Plant after the grade is checked with the level rod. Planting first just means digging them back up when the elevation turns out wrong.
lateNotes.curtain-turnbuckle: Tension the anchor after the curtain is laid across the reach — there is nothing to tension on a curtain that is not out yet.
lateNotes.silt-fence-panel: The fence goes up after the bench work is done — set first, it blocks the path the logs and bags still need to come in on.
lateNotes.turbidity-meter: Read turbidity after the curtain is tensioned. A reading against a slack curtain is not the baseline every log placement will be judged against.

name: Living Shoreline

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check today's low tide window and how much working time it actually gives you on the flat.
steps.prompt: Check today's low tide window and how much working time it actually gives you on the flat.
steps.title: Read the tide table before the first log goes in
steps.why: The whole day's sequence — curtain, logs, bags, plantings — is timed to a falling tide that exposes the toe of the bank and a rising one that will drown the same ground a few hours later. Reading the table first is what turns a full day of work into a plan instead of a race against water that was always coming back on its own schedule.

steps.cue: Read the Corps' 404 conditions, the BCDC permit, the Water Board's 401 certification, and the in-water work window.
steps.prompt: Read the Corps' 404 conditions, the BCDC permit, the Water Board's 401 certification, and the in-water work window.
steps.title: Check the permit conditions before work starts
steps.why: A Bay shoreline is worked under four signatures at once: the Corps' Clean Water Act (CWA) Section 404 permit, the Bay Conservation and Development Commission's own permit, the Regional Water Quality Control Board's 401 water quality certification, and a seasonal fish window that shuts the whole job down outside it. Missing any one of those conditions is not a paperwork problem — it is work that has to be undone.

steps.cue: Waders, a life vest, and gloves before anyone steps onto the flat.
steps.prompt: Waders, a life vest, and gloves before anyone steps onto the flat.
steps.title: Stage for working the tideline
steps.why: The footing here is soft mud over a falling tide, close enough to open water that a slip is a swim, not a stumble. Waders keep the cold bay water and whatever the mud is holding off skin that will be in it all day; the vest is buoyancy the moment the mud gives way; gloves are for the oyster shell and the wire on the coir bales, both of which cut clean through bare skin.

steps.cue: Walk the reach and click the three stakes the whole design is built from.

itemNotes.stake-1: Stake 1 marks the upstream end of the design reach. The coir toe starts here, not wherever the bank looks convenient this morning.
itemNotes.stake-2: Stake 2 is the mid-reach control — it is what tells the crew the toe line is still following the surveyed curve and not drifting straight.
itemNotes.stake-3: Stake 3 marks the downstream end. Past it, whatever gets placed is not part of the permitted design and does not count toward it.

steps.prompt: Walk the reach and click the three stakes the whole design is built from.
steps.title: Find the survey stakes that set the design template
steps.why: Everything that goes into this reach — curtain line, log toe, bag line, planting grade — is set against stakes a surveyor already put in, not against where the ground looks right today. Finding all three before anything is placed is what keeps four separate crew tasks building the same permitted design instead of four honest approximations of it.

steps.cue: Carry the curtain out and clip it along the line between the anchors.

drag.missNote: Not on the line — the curtain has to run the full width of the reach or the current finds the gap on the first ebb.

steps.prompt: Carry the curtain out and clip it along the line between the anchors.
steps.title: Deploy the turbidity curtain across the reach
steps.why: Every log placed and every root wad set stirs sediment into water that the 401 certification requires to stay inside a turbidity limit outside the work area. The curtain, marked and lit to Coast Guard (USCG) standard where it crosses open water, is what makes the difference between sediment that stays inside the work zone and sediment that becomes a violation the Water Board can measure from its own station downstream.

steps.cue: Wind the turnbuckle until the curtain skirt hangs plumb, not bellied out by the current.
steps.prompt: Wind the turnbuckle until the curtain skirt hangs plumb, not bellied out by the current.
steps.title: Tension the curtain's anchor turnbuckle
steps.why: A curtain that is only clipped on hangs loose the moment the tide starts moving water along the reach, and a loose curtain rides up off the bottom and lets everything under it go straight out with the ebb. The turnbuckle is what keeps the skirt down against a moving current instead of only against still water on a calm afternoon.

steps.cue: Take the reading and commit it against the permit's differential limit.

gauge.label: TURBIDITY
gauge.missNote: Outside the differential the permit allows. Let the reading settle against the outside station and commit inside the band.

steps.prompt: Take the reading and commit it against the permit's differential limit.
steps.title: Read turbidity inside the curtain against the outside station
steps.why: The 401 certification is not written against an absolute number — it is written against how much murkier the water inside the curtain is allowed to be than the water outside it. Reading it now, before the first log stirs anything, is what gives every reading taken for the rest of the day a real baseline to be judged against instead of a guess.

steps.cue: Place the coir logs against stakes 1, then 2, then 3, in that order.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Upstream to downstream — stake 1, then stake 2, then stake 3. A downstream log with nothing keyed above it takes load the design never asked it to carry alone.
steps.prompt: Place the coir logs against stakes 1, then 2, then 3, in that order.
steps.title: Set the coir logs to the stakes, upstream to downstream
steps.why: Coir logs are laid upstream first so each one keys against the log already down rather than leaving a gap the current finds on day one. Placed out of order, the downstream log takes the full force of water the upstream log was supposed to break first, and it is the one that moves on the next tide.

steps.cue: Set all three bags against the base of the coir, wherever the toe needs the extra armor.
steps.prompt: Set all three bags against the base of the coir, wherever the toe needs the extra armor.
steps.title: Place the oyster shell bags at the toe
steps.why: The shell bags are not a sequence the way the logs are — each one goes wherever the toe reads thinnest that day, judged by eye against the log that is already down. There is no fixed order to follow here, only three bags that all have to be down before the tide comes back over them.

steps.cue: Walk the root wad down the bench at a steady pull, holding it in the working range.
steps.holdBreakNote: The pull broke and the root wad settled into the mud short of the mark. Get the line taut again and bring it back to a steady pull.
steps.prompt: Walk the root wad down the bench at a steady pull, holding it in the working range.
steps.title: Haul the root wad anchor into position
steps.why: A root wad this size is muscled into place at a walking pace on a taut tag line, not muscled at a dead lift. Too fast and it swings and takes somebody's legs out from under them on wet ground; too slow and it drops into the mud and has to be dug back out before it can be moved another metre.

steps.cue: Read the rod against the design elevation and commit it in the planting band.

gauge.label: GRADE
gauge.missNote: Off the design elevation. Read the rod again at the marked point before a single plug goes in.

steps.prompt: Read the rod against the design elevation and commit it in the planting band.
steps.title: Check the planting grade with the level rod
steps.why: Cordgrass only survives in a narrow band of the tidal frame — too low and it drowns on every high tide, too high and it never gets wet enough to establish. The level rod read against the design elevation is the only thing standing between a planting that becomes marsh and one that becomes an expensive, short-lived lawn.

steps.cue: Hold each plug in and tamp the mud around it until the roots are seated.
steps.holdBreakNote: Let go before the mud closed around it — that plug is loose on the next tide. Reset it and hold until it is seated.
steps.prompt: Hold each plug in and tamp the mud around it until the roots are seated.
steps.title: Set the cordgrass plugs at grade
steps.why: A plug set at grade and let go immediately floats free on the next high water. Held and tamped until the mud closes back around the roots, it is anchored by the same tide everything else on this reach is built to work with instead of against.

steps.cue: Carry the fence panel to the line above the marsh bench and set the stakes.

drag.missNote: Not on the line — the fence has to run the full upland edge or the runoff finds the gap the same night it rains.

steps.prompt: Carry the fence panel to the line above the marsh bench and set the stakes.
steps.title: Install the silt fence at the upland edge
steps.why: The curtain protects the bay from what happens in the water; the silt fence protects the bay from what happens on the bank. Loose spoil and stockpiled soil have nowhere to go in a rainstorm except downhill into the same reach the curtain is guarding, so both controls are permit conditions and neither one substitutes for the other.

steps.cue: Look over everything placed today and click anything that will float off on the incoming tide.

itemNotes.drift-flag: A survey flag is pushed in by hand, not driven — this one is already leaning and will be floating free by the top of the flood.
itemNotes.loose-bag-tie: One shell bag's tie strap has come loose. Untied, the shell inside it is free to wash out of the bag and off the toe on the first real tide.

steps.prompt: Look over everything placed today and click anything that will float off on the incoming tide.
steps.title: Walk the reach before the flood
steps.why: The flood tide is the test nobody scheduled: it finds every strap that was not quite cinched and every stake that was pushed in by hand instead of driven home. Walking the reach now, on the falling tide, is the only chance anybody gets to fix what the water will otherwise take with it in a few hours.

tagline: Building a living shoreline on a falling tide: curtain set and tensioned, coir and oyster shell to the stakes, cordgrass at grade, silt fence at the edge, and the reach walked before the flood takes anything back
